text: Every az CLI command you've typed by hand so far prints straight to the terminal. This lesson turns that into a real script: a loop that checks every resource group in a subscription for a required tag, and reports exactly which ones are missing it — using the same bash you already know, just pointed at Azure.

The new piece is command substitution: dollar-sign-parentheses. RESOURCE_GROUPS equals dollar-paren az group list, with a query for just the name field and tsv output. That runs the command and hands its output back as a stored value instead of printing it, which is exactly what a for loop needs to work with.

Three pieces, none of them new. Command substitution captures az output as a value. --query and -o tsv are az's own filter and plain-text flag, flattening JSON down to one line per resource group. for and if are the identical loop and empty-string test from the shell-scripting basics you already covered.

Inside the loop, a second az call fetches one resource group's Environment tag: az group show, --name set to the current group, --query for tags.Environment. If that group has no such tag, the query returns nothing, and the bash test checking for an empty string catches it and reports MISSING instead of silently moving on.

Put together as check-tags.sh, the whole script is a shebang, one command substitution to list every resource group, a for loop, a second command substitution inside it to pull that group's tag, and an if/else that prints OK with the tag value or MISSING. chmod +x makes it runnable, and one pass checks every group in the subscription.

That's the same report a person would normally produce by clicking into each resource group's tags blade one at a time — except this version runs in seconds and never skips one. Next up: the identical bash pattern against the AWS CLI, checking EC2 instances instead of resource groups.
